item.title: Understanding email encryption — Fastmail
item.description:
• Source: https://www.fastmail.com/blog/email-encryption/
  • Author: Neil Jenkins
  • Site: Fastmail
  • Originally published: 2025-12-17
  • Date added: 2026-11-01

Summary

Fastmail's Neil Jenkins walks through the different layers of email encryption and what each actually protects against. TLS secures your connection to your provider, while server-to-server delivery relies on opportunistic TLS, which MTA-STS and DANE try to harden; Fastmail, like Google and Yahoo, prefers MTA-STS because DNSSEC failures can cause serious outages. Encryption at rest protects against physical theft but not court orders or full server compromise. Zero-access encryption (Proton, Tuta) limits insider access but leaves metadata exposed and costs search, standard clients, and password recovery, and true end-to-end encryption via S/MIME or PGP remains impractical for most people. The post's advice: for truly sensitive communication use Signal, and for everyday email, transport plus at-rest encryption is a sensible balance.

item.title: Building Effective Agents — Anthropic
item.description:
• Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents
  • Author: Erik S. and Barry Zhang (Anthropic)
  • Site: Anthropic Engineering
  • Originally published: 2024-12-19
  • Date added: 2026-10-22

Summary

Anthropic's widely shared engineering post (Dec 2024, by Erik S. and Barry Zhang) argues that the most successful LLM agents are built from simple, composable patterns rather than heavy frameworks. It distinguishes workflows (predefined code paths) from agents (models directing their own tool use), recommends starting with a single optimized LLM call and adding complexity only when it measurably helps, and walks through the augmented LLM plus five workflow patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer, before covering autonomous agents. Appendices cover where agents work well today (customer support, coding) and how to "prompt engineer" tools: easy formats, clear docs, and poka-yoke design. Note: the page says much of the tooling landscape has changed since it was written.
